items.q: Which processes are endothermic? Select all that apply.
options: Process A, dissolving calcium chloride
Process B, dissolving ammonium nitrate
Process C, magnesium in hydrochloric acid
Process D, baking soda in citric acid

items.q: Which statement describes the energy change in Process B?
options: Cold moves out of the dissolving solid into the water, so the water cools.
Energy moves from the water into the dissolving solid, so the water cools.
Energy moves from the dissolving solid into the water, so the water cools.
No energy moves; the water cools because the solid was colder to begin with.

items.q: What is the sign of ΔH for the reaction in Process C, and why?
options: Positive, because the water gained energy and its temperature rose
Positive, because a rising temperature means a positive change
Negative, because the reaction released energy that warmed the water
Zero, because the insulated cup kept the energy inside it

items.q: A classmate writes: "Process A is endothermic, because the solution absorbed heat and got warmer." Which correction is best?
options: The water warmed because the cup trapped energy from the air, so the process is neither.
The classmate is right, because any process that ends up warmer has taken in energy.
The process is endothermic, because dissolving a solid breaks its ions apart.
The water warmed because the dissolving released energy to it, so the process is exothermic.

items.q: Which process do the boxes show, and is it endothermic or exothermic?
options: Condensation; exothermic, because attractions form between the molecules
Vaporization; endothermic, because the molecules move closer together
Condensation; endothermic, because energy is needed to pull molecules together
A chemical reaction; exothermic, because new O–H bonds form inside each molecule

items.q: For the change from Box 1 to Box 2, which describes ΔH for the water?
options: ΔH is positive: the water takes energy from its surroundings.
ΔH is negative: the water gives energy to its surroundings.
ΔH is zero: the temperature is 100 °C in both boxes.
ΔH is positive: the O–H bonds inside each molecule get stronger.

items.q: The two boxes are at the same temperature. Where does the energy released during the change come from?
options: From the molecules moving faster in Box 2 than in Box 1
From covalent bonds breaking inside the water molecules
From the attractions that form between neighboring molecules
From the walls of the box, which push the molecules together

items.q: The change is now run backward, from Box 2 to Box 1, with the same amount of water. How does its ΔH compare with the forward change?
options: Same size and same sign: it is still exothermic.
Larger and positive, because the molecules also speed up.
Smaller and positive, because some attractions remain in the gas.
Same size, opposite sign: it is endothermic.

items.q: Which statement defines an exothermic process?
options: Energy leaves the system and enters the surroundings.
Energy leaves the surroundings and enters the system.
The temperature of the system stays the same.
The reaction needs a flame or spark to get started.

items.q: Which of these processes are exothermic? Select all that apply.
options: Liquid water freezing into ice
Ice melting on a countertop
Steam condensing on a cool bathroom mirror
Sweat evaporating from your skin
Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turning directly into gas
Natural gas (methane) burning on a stove

items.q: An ice cube at 0 °C is dropped into a well-insulated cup of water at 25 °C. Predict how each quantity changes over the next few minutes.

variables.name: Temperature of the liquid water around the ice
Energy of the ice as it melts
Total mass of the cup and its contents

items.q: After a run, sweat evaporates from an athlete's skin and she feels cooler. Which explanation is correct?
options: Evaporation is exothermic: the water releases its warmth into the air.
Sweat is colder than the skin, so it cools the skin by touching it.
Evaporation breaks O–H bonds, which takes energy from the skin.
Evaporation is endothermic: separating water molecules absorbs energy from the skin.

items.q: A student says, "Breaking a chemical bond releases energy, which is why fuels give off energy when they burn." Which statement corrects this?
options: Breaking a bond absorbs energy; energy is released when new, stronger bonds form in the products.
Breaking a bond releases energy, but just for bonds with a high bond energy.
Breaking a bond releases energy in fuels, but absorbs energy in other substances.
Breaking and forming bonds involve no energy; temperature changes do.

items.q: A reaction mixture in a flask becomes hot to the touch. Which statement about the bonds is consistent with this observation?
options: Breaking the reactant bonds released more energy than forming the product bonds absorbed.
Forming the product bonds released more energy than breaking the reactant bonds absorbed.
Breaking the reactant bonds absorbed more energy than forming the product bonds released.
No bonds broke or formed, since the energy came from the flask itself.

items.q: Solid barium hydroxide octahydrate and solid ammonium chloride are mixed in a flask that sits in a puddle of water on a wooden board. Soon the puddle freezes, sticking the flask to the board. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The reaction releases cold into the puddle, so ΔH < 0.
The reaction releases energy into the puddle, so ΔH < 0.
The reaction absorbs energy from the flask, the puddle and the board, so ΔH > 0.
The puddle freezes by itself, so the reaction has ΔH = 0.

items.q: A student dissolves sodium hydroxide pellets in water. Which observation is evidence that dissolving them is exothermic?
options: The pellets get smaller and disappear as they are stirred.
The solution conducts electricity once the pellets have dissolved.
The mass of the solution equals the mass of water plus pellets.
A thermometer in the water reads a higher temperature than before.

items.q: In a chemistry lab, which choice treats a reaction in a beaker of water the way chemists usually do?
options: The reacting particles are the system; the water, beaker and air are the surroundings.
The water is the system, because its temperature is what the thermometer measures.
The beaker and its contents are the system; the room air is the surroundings.
The thermometer is the system, since its reading is what changes.

items.q: Which statement about enthalpy change, ΔH, is correct?
options: ΔH is positive when the surroundings get warmer.
ΔH is positive when the system absorbs energy at constant pressure.
ΔH is the temperature change of the system, in degrees Celsius.
ΔH is negative when energy has to be added to keep a process going.

items.q: Use the diagram to determine ΔH for the reaction X + Y → Z, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted products from reactants. ΔH is products minus reactants, and the products here are lower, so ΔH is negative.
Value: that is the activation energy, the climb from the reactants to the peak. ΔH compares the two flat ends.

items.q: Use the diagram to determine the activation energy of the forward reaction, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you measured from the products to the peak, which is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
Value: you read the height of the peak. The activation energy is the climb from the reactants up to the peak.

items.q: Which statement about the reverse reaction, Z → X + Y, is supported by the diagram?
options: It is exothermic, with ΔH = −87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 89 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 89 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 176 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of zero.

items.q: A catalyst is added to the reaction mixture. How does the diagram change?
options: The peak is lower, and the products move down, so ΔH becomes more negative.
The peak stays the same, and the products move down, so more energy is released.
The peak is higher, so the reaction absorbs extra energy and ΔH becomes positive.
The peak is lower; the reactant and product levels, and so ΔH, stay the same.

items.q: Which reactions are endothermic? Select all that apply.
options: Reaction P
Reaction Q
Reaction R
Reaction S

items.q: Which reaction has the largest activation energy in the forward direction?
options: Reaction P, with the largest increase in enthalpy overall
Reaction R, with a climb of 130 kJ/mol
Reaction S, because its hump is at 150 kJ
Reaction Q, because it releases the most energy

items.q: Reactions P and Q have the same size of ΔH. What does the diagram data show about them?
options: Both release 60 kJ per mole of reaction, because the size of ΔH is the same.
Both absorb 60 kJ per mole of reaction, because each hump is above its reactants.
P absorbs 60 kJ per mole of reaction and Q releases 60 kJ, so their signs are opposite.
They have the same activation energy, because they have the same size of ΔH.

items.q: Determine the activation energy, in kJ/mol, of the reverse of Reaction R (products → reactants).

mistakes.why: Value: that is the forward activation energy, measured from the reactants. The reverse climb starts at the products.
Value: you read the height of the hump. The activation energy is the climb from the starting level up to the hump.

items.q: On an energy diagram, where is ΔH of a reaction shown?
options: As the vertical distance from the reactant level to the product level
As the vertical distance from the reactant level to the top of the hump
As the horizontal length of the curve from start to finish
As the height of the top of the hump above the axis

items.q: A diagram for the reaction 2 H₂O₂(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g), which warms the solution, is drawn by a student with the products higher than the reactants. What is wrong?
options: The products belong at the same level as the reactants, because atoms are conserved.
A reaction that warms its surroundings releases energy, so its products belong below the reactants.
Nothing is wrong, because a reaction that warms its surroundings gains enthalpy.
The hump is missing, because a reaction that releases energy has no activation energy.

items.q: Which energy diagram matches an endothermic reaction that is fast at room temperature?
options: Products well below the reactants, with a small hump
Products a little above the reactants, with a very tall hump
Products a little above the reactants, with a small hump
Products level with the reactants, with no hump

items.q: A reaction has ΔH = −45 kJ/mol and a forward activation energy of 70 kJ/mol. The reaction is run backward instead. Predict how each value compares with the forward reaction.
Methane burns in oxygen with ΔH = −890 kJ/mol, yet a gas stove does not light until a spark is applied. Which energy diagram explains both facts?
options: Products far below reactants, with a hump that the spark helps the molecules climb
Products far above reactants, so the spark supplies the extra energy stored in the products
Products far below reactants, with no hump, so the spark is not really needed
Products level with reactants, with a hump that the spark climbs

items.q: Which pair of quantities can be read from an energy diagram without any other data?
options: The sign of ΔH and the temperature at which the reaction is run
The sign of ΔH and whether the forward Ea is larger than the reverse Ea
The rate constant and the time the reaction takes to finish
The mass of products formed and the mass of reactants used

items.q: For an exothermic elementary reaction, how do the forward and reverse activation energies compare?
options: The forward Ea is larger, by the size of ΔH
They are equal, because both directions pass over the same hump
The reverse Ea is larger, by the size of ΔH
The reverse Ea is zero, because the reverse reaction absorbs energy

items.q: At what time do the block and the water first reach thermal equilibrium?
options: At about 240 s, when both read 29.4 °C
At 0 s, when the block is placed in the water
At about 90 s, when the block's temperature stops falling quickly
At about 120 s, when the water reaches 29.4 °C

items.q: Why does the block's temperature fall fastest in the first 30 s?
options: The water is coldest then, so it releases cold into the block fastest.
The temperature difference is largest then, so energy moves from block to water fastest.
The block holds the most thermal energy at the start, so it gives most of it away in the first seconds.
The block is still being heated during the first 30 s.

items.q: The block's temperature drops by 65.6 °C, while the water's rises by only 8.4 °C. Which statement explains this, assuming no energy leaves the container?
options: The block loses much more energy than the water gains, since its temperature changes more.
The water gains energy from the container, so it needs less from the block.
The block loses exactly the energy the water gains, but that energy changes the water's temperature less.
Some of the block's energy is destroyed as it cools, so the water gains less.

items.q: Later calculations show that the block lost 7.06 kJ of energy between 0 s and 300 s. How much energy, in kJ, did the water gain, if no energy left the container?

mistakes.why: Sign: the water gained energy, so its energy change is positive. The block's change is −7.06 kJ.

items.q: Which gas is at the higher temperature at the moment shown?
options: Gas A, because its particles have the greater average speed
Gas B, because its particles are slower and so hold more energy
They are at the same temperature, because each chamber has eight particles
Gas B, because it is on the side that will receive energy

items.q: How does energy pass from one gas to the other through the wall?
options: Particles of A pass through tiny gaps in the wall and mix with gas B, carrying their extra kinetic energy along with them.
Fast particles of A hit the wall and make its atoms vibrate more, which then speed up the particles of B that hit it.
Slow particles of B pass their cold through the wall to A.
The wall releases its own stored energy into both gases equally.

items.q: Predict how each quantity changes after a long time, once the gases reach thermal equilibrium.

variables.name: Average speed of the particles of A
Average speed of the particles of B
Number of particles in each chamber
Total energy of the two gases together

items.q: Once the gases reach thermal equilibrium, which statement is true at the particle level?
options: Each particle in both gases now moves at the same speed as the particles next to it, with no spread of speeds left.
Particles stop colliding with the wall, so no energy moves.
Energy keeps flowing from A to B, but more slowly.
Particles still collide with the wall, but energy passes in both directions at equal rates.

items.q: A spoon at 22 °C is put into a cup of tea at 80 °C. Which describes what happens?
options: Energy flows from the tea to the spoon until both reach the same temperature.
Cold flows from the spoon into the tea until both reach the same temperature.
Energy flows from the spoon to the tea until the spoon reaches 80 °C.
No energy flows, because a metal and a liquid do not exchange energy.

items.q: Which is the best definition of heat in chemistry?
options: The total kinetic energy of the particles that make up a hot object or sample
Energy transferred between objects because of a difference in temperature
A measure of how fast the particles in an object are moving
A substance that flows out of hot objects into cold ones

items.q: On a cold morning, a metal bench feels colder than a wooden bench, though both are at 2 °C. Which explanation is correct?
options: The metal is at a lower temperature than the wood.
The metal gives off cold more quickly than the wood does.
Metal transfers energy away from your skin faster than wood does.
The wood is warming your skin, while the metal is not.

items.q: In an insulated container, a warm copper block loses 1.85 kJ of energy to cool water. The water ends at the same temperature as the block. How much energy, in J, did the water gain?

mistakes.why: Units: 1.85 is the energy in kJ. The question asks for joules: multiply by 1000 J/kJ.
Sign: the water gained energy, so its value is positive. The copper's change is −1850 J.

items.q: In an insulated cup, 100 g of water at 60 °C is mixed with 100 g of water at 20 °C. What is the final temperature?
A hot iron nail and a cool block of the same mass of iron are placed in contact in an insulated box. Which final temperature is possible if the nail started at 90 °C and the block at 30 °C?
A student says, "When ice cools a drink, the ice is giving cold to the drink." Which statement corrects this at the particle level?
options: The ice's slow particles collide with the drink and pass their slowness to it.
The drink cools because the ice removes particles from the drink.
The drink's faster particles collide with the ice and lose energy to it, so the drink cools.
The drink cools because the ice makes the cup lose energy to the room.

items.q: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium with each other. What must be true?
options: They contain the same amount of thermal energy.
They are made of the same substance.
Their particles have the same mass.
They are at the same temperature, so there is no net energy flow between them.

items.q: Calculate the energy, in kJ, gained by the solution in the calorimeter.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the mass of one solution (50.0 g). Both solutions are in the cup and both warm up, so use the combined 100.0 g.
Value: you used the final temperature instead of the change. ΔT = highest temperature − starting temperature.

items.q: How many moles of water are formed in the reaction?

mistakes.why: Value: you added the moles of acid and base. They react 1 : 1, so 0.0500 mol of each makes 0.0500 mol of water.
Value: convert mL to L before multiplying by the molarity (mol/L).

items.q: Calculate ΔH for the reaction, in kJ per mole of water formed.

mistakes.why: Sign: the solution warmed, so the reaction released energy. ΔH of the reaction is negative: q(reaction) = −q(solution).
Value: you divided by 0.100 mol, the moles of acid plus base. Divide by the moles of water formed, 0.0500 mol.
Value: that is the energy for this sample. ΔH per mole means dividing by the moles of water formed, 0.0500 mol.

items.q: The student repeats the trial in a single uncovered cup, so some energy escapes to the room. How does the calculated ΔH compare with the first result?
options: More negative, because the reaction releases more energy in an open cup
Unchanged, because the same amounts of acid and base react
Positive, because energy now flows from the cup into the room
Less negative, because the measured temperature rise is smaller

items.q: The student then mixes 100.0 mL of each 1.00 M solution instead of 50.0 mL. Which prediction is correct?
options: The temperature rise is about the same, and so is ΔH per mole of water.
The temperature rise doubles, but ΔH per mole of water stays the same.
The temperature rise doubles, and ΔH per mole of water doubles too.
The temperature rise halves, because the energy spreads through more solution.

items.q: Which value should the student use for ΔT of the solution?
options: −3.13 °C, from 22.40 °C to the last reading, 19.27 °C
−3.36 °C, from 22.40 °C to the lowest point, 19.04 °C
19.04 °C, the lowest temperature reached
−1.10 °C, the drop in the first 15 s after adding the solid

items.q: Calculate the energy, in kJ, that the solution lost while the solid dissolved.

mistakes.why: Value: you used 100.0 g of water alone. The dissolved solid is part of the solution that cooled, so the mass is 100.0 g + 5.35 g.

items.q: Calculate ΔH for dissolving NH₄Cl, in kJ per mole of NH₄Cl.

mistakes.why: Sign: the solution cooled, so the dissolving absorbed energy. ΔH is positive: q(dissolving) = −q(solution).
Value: you divided by the mass in grams. ΔH per mole needs the moles of NH₄Cl: mass ÷ molar mass.

items.q: Which statement gives the correct signs for this experiment?
options: q for the solution is negative and q for the dissolving is positive.
q for the solution is positive and q for the dissolving is negative.
Both are negative, because the temperature went down.
Both are positive, because energy was transferred.

items.q: After 150 s, the temperature slowly rises. Which explanation fits the data?
options: The dissolved NH₄Cl starts releasing the energy it absorbed earlier.
Energy from the warmer room leaks into the cold solution through the cup.
The solid begins to dissolve faster, which warms the solution.
The thermometer warms the solution because of its own heat capacity.

items.q: What does it mean that liquid water has a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g·°C)?
options: It takes 4.18 J to raise the temperature of 1 mol of water by 1 °C.
1 g of water at 4.18 °C has 1 J of energy.
It takes 4.18 J to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C.
Water boils after it absorbs 4.18 J per gram.

items.q: A 52.5 g piece of metal at 99.20 °C is placed in 75.0 g of water at 21.30 °C in a calorimeter. Both end at 26.48 °C. Assuming all the energy lost by the metal is gained by the water, find the specific heat of the metal, in J/(g·°C).

The ΔH°f result, because those values are measured for the actual substances, not averaged.
The bond-enthalpy result, because ΔH°f values ignore the bonds broken.

items.q: A student calculates ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) and gets +890.3 kJ/mol. Which errors could explain it? Select all that apply.
options: Subtracting products from reactants instead of reactants from products
Using ΔH°f of H₂O(g) instead of H₂O(l)
Including ΔH°f = 0 for O₂
Leaving out the coefficient 2 on water

items.q: What must the student do with Reaction 3 to use it toward the target?
options: Reverse it, so CH₄ appears as a product; ΔH becomes +890.3 kJ/mol.
Reverse it, so CH₄ appears as a product; ΔH stays −890.3 kJ/mol.
Keep it exactly as written, since CH₄ already appears in Reaction 3.
Multiply it by 2, since the target has 2 H₂.

items.q: Use Hess's law to calculate ΔH° for C(graphite) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g), in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: Reaction 3 must be reversed, so its ΔH becomes +890.3 kJ/mol, not −890.3.
Value: Reaction 2 already has 2 H₂, as the target does; use it as written, without halving.
Sign: you reversed the wrong reactions. Keep 1 and 2 as written (C and H₂ are reactants in the target) and reverse 3.

items.q: Which substances cancel when the three adjusted reactions are added? Select all that apply.
options: O₂(g)
CO₂(g)
H₂O(l)
H₂(g)
CH₄(g)
C(graphite)

items.q: Why is the answer the same as the standard enthalpy of formation of CH₄(g)?
options: Any answer found with Hess's law is the enthalpy of formation of the last product.
CH₄ is an element, so its ΔH°f is the value of any reaction it is in.
The three measured reactions are each formation reactions.
The target makes 1 mol of CH₄ from its elements in their standard states.

items.q: What is ΔH for Route A, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: ΔH₂ is −114.2 kJ/mol; add it with its sign.
Sign: you reversed the steps. Both are used as written, since they already lead from N₂ + O₂ to NO₂.

items.q: Which statement explains why Route A and Route B must have the same overall ΔH?
options: Both routes involve the same number of steps, so they have the same ΔH.
Enthalpy is a state function: its change depends only on the starting and final states.
Energy is created in Step 1 and then destroyed in Step 2, so the two routes balance out.
Both routes happen at the same speed, so they release the same energy.

items.q: What is ΔH for 2 NO₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2 O₂(g)?
options: +66.4 kJ/mol
−33.2 kJ/mol
−66.4 kJ/mol
−180.6 kJ/mol

items.q: What is ΔH, in kJ/mol, for NO(g) + ½ O₂(g) → NO₂(g)?

mistakes.why: Value: Step 2 makes 2 mol of NO₂. Halving the equation halves ΔH.
Sign: halving does not change the sign; only reversing does.

items.q: Which statement is Hess's law?
options: If a reaction is the sum of steps, its ΔH is the sum of the steps' ΔH values.
ΔH of a reaction equals the activation energy of its slowest step.
ΔH of a multistep reaction is the same as the ΔH of its first step alone.
ΔH doubles each time a reaction is split into two separate steps.

items.q: Given 4 Al(s) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 Al₂O₃(s), ΔH = −3351.4 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for 2 Al(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s)?
Given S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −296.8 kJ/mol, and S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g), ΔH = −395.7 kJ/mol, find ΔH for SO₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → SO₃(g), in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: SO₂ is a reactant in the target, so reverse the first equation (+296.8 kJ/mol).
Sign: you reversed the wrong equation. SO₃ is a product in the target, so keep the second as written.

items.q: Use Hess's law to find ΔH for 2 C(graphite) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g), given: (1) C₂H₂(g) + 5/2 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), ΔH = −1300.0 kJ/mol; (2) C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ/mol; (3) H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: the target has 2 C, so multiply equation (2) and its ΔH by 2.
Sign: C₂H₂ is a product in the target, so reverse equation (1): +1300.0 kJ/mol.
Sign: check which equations to reverse. Only (1) is reversed.

items.q: A student reverses an equation for a Hess's law problem and multiplies it by 2, then uses ΔH = −2 × (+150 kJ/mol). What did the student get, and is it right?
options: −300 kJ/mol, which is right: reversing flips the sign and doubling doubles the size.
+300 kJ/mol, which is right: reversing and doubling cancel each other's effect on the sign.
−150 kJ/mol, which is wrong: the reversal alone should change ΔH.
+150 kJ/mol, which is wrong: ΔH stays the same when an equation is rearranged.

items.q: Which quantity is a state function?
options: The distance a hiker walks to the top of a hill
The enthalpy of a system
The total energy a stove burns while cooking a meal
The number of steps in a reaction mechanism

items.q: Three methods give ΔH for one reaction: a coffee-cup measurement (−52.0 kJ/mol), Hess's law from tabulated reactions (−56.0 kJ/mol), and bond enthalpies (−61 kJ/mol). Which explanation of the differences is best?
options: Hess's law gives a different ΔH, because routing through other reactions changes the total energy.
The bond-enthalpy value is the most exact, because it counts the actual bonds broken and formed.
Energy lost from the cup makes the measurement low, and average bond enthalpies make that estimate least exact.
The three should agree exactly, so any difference between them means a calculation mistake was made.

items.q: Put the steps for solving a Hess's law problem in order.
options: Write the target equation and note which side each substance is on.
Reverse any given equation whose substance is on the wrong side, and change the sign of its ΔH.
Multiply equations so the amounts match the target, and multiply each ΔH by the same factor.
Add the adjusted equations and check that everything not in the target cancels.
Add the adjusted ΔH values to get ΔH of the target.
